title: Runtime degradation response playbook
content:
Purpose and scope
This is a lightweight on-call runbook for handling short-to-medium-duration runtime degradations that affect the inference API surface: request timeouts, quota/429 spikes, degraded streaming (partial payloads, stalls), and elevated 5xx/4xx error rates. The goal is to provide quick triage steps, pragmatic mitigations (keep apps alive with graceful degradation), and a checklist for follow-up analysis. This is a working draft — add notes from each incident after handoff.

When to use this playbook
- Pager or alert fires for: sustained latency above SLO for >2 min, >=3x normal 429 rate within 5m window, streaming error rate spike, or steady increase in 5xx rate.
- If the issue appears to be a single-tenant config problem, follow tenant-specific containment first (see tenant isolation below).

Signals and thresholds (examples we use in Grafana/Prometheus)
- API p95 latency for /v1/outputs > 1.5 * SLO for 5+ minutes
  PromQL: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job=\"redwood-api\"}[5m])) by (le, route))
- 429 rate spike: sum(rate(http_requests_total{code=\"429\"}[1m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[1m])) > 0.03 (3%) sustained
- Streaming stall: percent of connections with >2s inter-chunk gap > 1%
  Derived from streaming_heartbeat_gap_seconds metric and connection counts.
- Elevated 5xx: rate(http_requests_total{code=~\"5..\"}[5m]) increased > 2x baseline

Quick context collection (first 3 minutes)
- Scope: global vs region vs model vs tenant? Check per-route breakdown in Grafana.
- Severity: impacting production traffic (>5% global error/latency drift) vs localized (single region/model/tenant).
- Recent deploys/rollouts: check CI/CD deployment stream for any canary/rollout in last 30m (GitHub Actions / Spinnaker / Argo events).
- Capacity signals: GPU/host CPU pressure, queue backlog, network errors.
- Any active mitigation already (traffic shaping, fallback model, rate-limits increased)?

Quick dashboard queries and commands (copy/paste)
- Per-route p95: Grafana panel or PromQL above.
- 429 by route: sum by(route)(rate(http_requests_total{code=\"429\"}[1m]))
- Top offending models: sum by(model)(rate(requests_total{status!~\"2..\"}[5m]))
- Kubernetes pod restart/history: kubectl -n runtime get pods -l app=redwood-runtime -o wide
- Tail streaming proxy logs (last 200 lines): kubectl -n runtime logs svc/stream-proxy -c proxy --tail=200
- Short curl smoke test (non-streaming): curl -s -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/outputs -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TEST' -d '{"input":"smoke test"}' | jq .

Triage flow by failure mode
1) Timeouts (request does not complete / long queuing)
  - Symptoms: high p95/p99, requests hanging in queue, worker queue length increases.
  - Quick checks:
    * Check per-worker queue length: curl -s http://runtime-internal/metrics | grep worker_queue_size
    * Check GPU utilization and pending queue on scheduler: kubectl top nodes; check scheduler queue metric scheduler_pending_requests
    * Are KV caches warm? Large cold-cache storms can spike latency — check kv_cache_hit_ratio metric.
  - Immediate mitigations:
    * Enable degraded response mode: toggle config 'prefer_fast_path=true' on the runtime-config map for affected replica set (this disables some quality-heavy postprocessing).
    * If queue is backed up, scale up target pool (if Dedicated) or bring up burst nodes: patch autoscaler minReplicas + deploy extra nodes.
    * As short-term: reduce per-request max_tokens or max_context to lower compute per request for high-load routes (via the route override API).
  - If root cause appears as slow model kernels: failover to a compatible smaller/quantized model (see routing fallback rules).

2) 429s / quota spikes
  - Symptoms: elevated 429s across clients, often coupled with sudden traffic increase or misbehaving client.
  - Quick checks:
    * Identify top source keys: sum by(api_key)(rate(http_requests_total{code=\"429\"}[1m]))
    * Check recent config changes to rate-limiter or quota buckets.
    * Inspect request patterns: are there many small rapid requests or heavy batch requests?
  - Immediate mitigations:
    * Apply temporary per-key throttles for noisy clients via rate-limit overrides in the WAF/rate-limiter UI.
    * Open a short-term emergency quota increase for critical customers if caused by legitimate load and capacity exists.
    * Activate soft-fallback: route best-effort traffic to a lower-cost tier/model with permissive rate limit so customer requests still complete with degraded quality.
  - If due to exploit/noisy client: identify and block offending IPs/keys; issue customer outreach for aggressive clients.

3) Degraded streaming (partial output, stalls, chunk gaps)
  - Symptoms: clients report cut-off responses, long inter-chunk gaps, or aborted connections.
  - Quick checks:
    * Inspect streaming proxy metrics: streaming_chunks_sent_total, streaming_chunk_gap_seconds_bucket
    * Check connection counts and socket errors on edge LB and proxy layer
    * Look for memory pressure on proxy which can delay flushes (proxy_gc_pauses_seconds)
  - Immediate mitigations:
    * Restart offending stream-proxy pods (rolling restart one-by-one) to clear stuck connections if proxy memory/FD leak suspected.
    * Route streaming traffic to alternate proxies/regions using smart-routing (route-rule: prefer-region:us-west-2 or fallback to streaming-lite variant).
    * If chunk serialization is slow (large attachments), enforce chunk-size cap at ingress for the short term.
  - Post-incident: add deeper hooks to capture per-connection timelines and chunk latencies to S3 for replay.

4) Elevated 5xx error rates (model runtime errors, OOMs, fatal kernel traps)
  - Symptoms: surge in 5xx across routes, repeated container OOM kills, or model-serving process exits.
  - Quick checks:
    * kubectl -n runtime get pods -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, restarts: .status.containerStatuses[].restartCount, reason: .status.containerStatuses[].state.waiting.reason}'
    * Check node kubelet logs for OOM or docker/CRI errors.
  - Immediate mitigations:
    * Isolate bad model variant: scale down pods serving that model and shift traffic to fallback model variants.
    * If OOMs: temporarily increase memory requests on pod spec and roll. Use preemptive cordon if node shows repeated OOM behavior.
    * If due to new rollout: rollback the rollout immediately and pin previous model version.

Containment guidance (tenant isolation)
- If a single tenant is triggering noise: use tenant isolation endpoint to move that tenant to a drained pool (drain-tenant --tenant-id <id>), and create a dedicated low-priority queue for them. This preserves global capacity.
- For managed Dedicated customers: coordinate with account engineer before killing any customer-dedicated nodes.

Escalation matrix and communication
- On-call SRE -> if not resolved in 15 minutes or if customer-impacting: notify SRE lead (Marco Rivera) and on-call product PM.
- Use #sre-incident Slack channel and update triage summary every 10 minutes until stable.
- Customer-facing comms: Customer Success drafts initial "we are investigating" note. Avoid technical details; provide ETA and mitigation status.

Post-incident tasks (owner within 48h)
- Full autopsy: gather traces, logs, and the top 20 affected requests.
- Root cause analysis draft: timeline, contributing factors, and concrete action items (no nested action items here — track in JIRA).
- Add or tune alerts to reduce noisy signals and add runbook links to each alert.
- If fallback was used: create a follow-up plan to validate fallback quality and rollback criteria.

Runbook maintenance notes (TODOs)
- Add exact kubectl/helm commands for our internal clusters (sensitive commands should live in Ops Playbook, link in Confluence).
- Instrumentation: we need a derived metric for per-request compute-seconds to better catch heavy requests before they affect latency.
- Postmortem template: include a section for "customer-level impact" and "cost delta during mitigation".

Unresolved questions to capture during incidents
- Are we consistently measuring streaming stutters at the proxy vs the model process? (Ambiguity causes slow RCA.)
- Should we gate large-context requests behind a separate priority queue?
- What is acceptable degraded quality fallback for enterprise customers vs self-serve?

Notes from recent incidents (live log)
- 2024-09-10: Short-lived 429 spike traced to a bug in batcher that duplicated requests during retry window. Mitigation: throttled offending batcher, deployed fix in batch dedupe logic (PR-842).
- 2024-10-02: Streaming stalls after edge-proxy GC pauses; rolling restart of proxy fixed immediate issue. Action: add heap-pressure alerts and tune GC.

End of playbook.
Add any new on-call observations below this line after each incident for continuous improvement.
